maududi-response-to-atheism.title: How Maududi answered atheism
maududi-response-to-atheism.lede: When atheistic ideas reached the Indian subcontinent in the 20th century, Maulana Maududi answered them in writing. The paper surveys his methods and the Qur'anic arguments he relied on.
body: In the 20th century, atheistic ideas began to spread in the Indian subcontinent alongside modern Western civilisation. The paper defines atheistic thought broadly: denying God's existence, aversion to religion, so-called free thinking, rejecting God's attributes, and a general drift away from faith. Scholars of the time stood firm against it, and one of the best known was Maulana Syed Abul A'la Maududi, who met these challenges with scholarship and research.

According to the authors, Maududi produced a reasoned and wide-ranging body of writing to answer the objections raised by modern civilisation and by atheism, and he used different methods to reach different parts of society. The paper credits these efforts with bringing many young people back to the teachings of Islam. It works through a series of objections, including doubts about God's existence, about resurrection and the afterlife, and about revelation, and draws mainly on Maududi's own works, among them his Qur'an commentary, Tafhim al-Qur'an.

Maududi's answers lean heavily on the Qur'an. On God's existence, the paper cites the verse asking how people can disbelieve in Allah when they were lifeless and He gave them life, will cause them to die, and will bring them to life again (2:28). On resurrection, it cites the challenge of the one who asks who could give life to bones once they have decayed, and the reply that He who made them the first time will revive them (36:78–79), together with a hadith that every servant will be raised in the state in which he died. On revelation, it cites the verse that the Prophet does not speak from his own desire (53:3). Elsewhere it draws on verses about the signs in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of night and day (3:190), the purpose of creating jinn and humankind (51:56), and the Qur'an guiding to what is most upright (17:9).

The authors conclude that through these methods, combining Qur'an-based argument, careful reasoning and approaches suited to different audiences, Maududi fulfilled an important intellectual and scholarly responsibility: answering the objections and doubts raised by the atheistic thought of his time.
points: Atheistic ideas reached the Indian subcontinent in the 20th century with modern Western civilisation.
Maududi answered them with a large body of reasoned writing aimed at different audiences.
His replies on God, resurrection and revelation rest heavily on Qur'anic verses.
The authors credit his work with bringing many young people back to Islam's teachings.
maududi-response-to-atheism.notes: The paper is in Urdu; only the title and abstract are in English, and the PDF extraction of the Urdu body is badly garbled. The summary rests on the English abstract plus the Arabic verse and hadith citations and footnotes that survived extraction. The list of objections (God's existence, resurrection/afterlife, revelation) is read from the few legible section headings and the verses cited under them; there appear to be further sections (possibly on Islamic rulings and on religion's place in life) that could not be read, so they are left out. The verses are paraphrased because the paper's own (Urdu) translations are unreadable. The name Tafhim al-Qur'an is inferred from a garbled footnote with the publisher Idara Tarjuman al-Qur'an. Someone who reads Urdu should check the original before publishing. Blurb is accurate.
